speakers.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: To ask His Majesty’s Government what steps they are taking to enhance provision for the teaching of citizenship.
contributions.name: Lord Norton of Louth

contributions.text: My Lords, at the weekend the noble Lord, Ricketts, warned of the threats posed by hybrid attacks on our national infrastructure. The threats are growing and becoming more dangerous. They threaten our very system of government and the values that underpin it. We are vulnerable because of the spread of disinformation and false narratives, not least through social media. Many people, especially young people, lack the critical capacity to interrogate the veracity of what is posted and lack an understanding of how our system works and what it delivers to them and to society as a whole. The pervasive use of social media also serves to undermine community engagement, with people no longer coming together to pursue their interests and engage in social discourse. The dissemination of fake news by malign sources, whether domestic or foreign, serves to undermine trust in our political system and culture. The 2023 ONS Trust in g overnment survey found that a majority of those questioned, 57%, had low or no trust in both government and Parliament. Our system of government, how we choose to govern ourselves and the values that underpin a healthy polity—adherence to the rule of law, justice and t
contributions.name: Lord Norton of Louth

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Norton, and I agreed with every word he said. I thank him for referring to the 2018 Select Committee on which I served. In the very short time available, I will make just three points. First, it is excellent that the officials from the Department for Education are working extremely well with the Association of Citizenship Teaching, of which I am a long-standing honorary president, to make sure that we get the materials right and that we ensure that the teaching is of the quality that we would wish. Secondly, I welcome the work of the Electoral Commission and the materials that it is putting out over the current year and into 2028, but I ask that it co-ordinates with the work of the department and the revised citizenship curriculum, so that it makes sense not just in schools and colleges but to post-16 young people who are not in those formal settings. Thirdly, we should bring forward the revised citizenship curriculum to 2027. It is possible, speaking as a former Education and Employment Secretary and someone who has taught in further education, to bring forward parts of that revised curriculum to September next year in time to inform, educate
contributions.name: Lord Blunkett

contributions.text: My Lords, it is a pleasure to follow the noble Lord, Lord Blunkett, given that the University of Sheffield and Bernard Crick in particular were leaders in talking about citizenship education. Earlier this year, ahead of the Representation of the People Bill reaching our House, I visited a number of secondary schools in London and Yorkshire to ask how they planned to adjust their curriculum to prepare students to exercise their vote from 16. I was shaken by how little time any of them currently had for education about democracy, law and citizenship, including in one of England’s leading independent schools. One hour a week for all aspects of personal development—personal relationships, finance, drugs, online stress, fakes and misinformation, bullying and grooming, health, careers, British values and democracy—is a crazy race through too many important topics. The students I met admitted how little they knew about political issues but were very keen to know more. After the first Reform Act, the Earl of Eldon argued in a debate in this House against educating the working classes as it would give them ideas above their station. A recent Telegraph op-ed argued similarly that political e
contributions.name: Lord Wallace of Saltaire

contributions.text: My Lords, in our Church of England schools, we are proud of the role we play in preparing young people of all faiths and none to participate thoughtfully, respectfully and confidently in our diverse arena of public life. However, many of our schools serve small, rural communities, and therefore have far less flexibility when it comes to specialist staffing. In light of the Government’s decision to lower the voting age, can the Minister say what steps will be taken to ensure that all schools are adequately resourced to deliver the high-quality citizenship education that young people will need to fulfil this new responsibility? We should also afford sufficient attention to the programme of study for key stage 1. We want our youngest children to recognise the difference between right and wrong, to understand that they belong to various communities and to realise that people and other living things have a responsibility to each other. By grounding early education in these fundamental values, we can foster an environment of fellowship with one another that enables human flourishing and invests in a bright future for our communities. We should not treat early citizenship learning as an a
contributions.name: The Lord Bishop of Peterborough

contributions.text: My Lords, I strongly agree with my noble friend Lord Norton of Louth that citizenship education should extend deeply into other bodies engaged in civil society. As we know, all politics is basically local politics, and as a very long-standing local resident in the City of Westminster I am glad to see that Westminster City Council now has a deputy cabinet member designated for civic matters—indeed, for civic pride. That is a very good thing for local authorities to turn their attention to in order to shore up the key values of our British polity. Providentially, this debate comes at a critical time for the peaceful polity of many countries in Europe and beyond, such as India, where in recent weeks we have seen a lot of uncivil youthquakes bursting out all over their societies—tragically, particularly in France. I have seen these maybe harmless student demonstrations being suddenly transmogrified into something very much more serious, with savage assaults on the very ideal of fraternity and the free benefits of education in civil society. Mercifully, we in the UK have been spared this sort of thing, and long may that last. We must spread the message as quickly as possible, starting w
contributions.name: Lord Patten

contributions.text: My Lords, the upcoming national curriculum reforms, making citizenship compulsory in primary schools and deepening focus on democracy and media literacy in secondary schools, are an excellent step forward. However, you can teach the mechanics of a democratic system, but you cannot put in a syllabus the courage it takes to step up and use them. True citizenship requires us to step completely out of our comfort zones. When I look back at my own journey, my real integration into society did not just happen in a classroom. It happened when I forced myself into unfamiliar spaces. Joining team sports and the school orchestra taught me how to co-operate with completely different groups of people. Later, the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award pushed me even further. It led me to the doorstep of an elderly lady. Every week, I did her shopping and simply sat and spoke with her. That single step out of my own world gave me a profound, real-world understanding of my local community. It taught me empathy, history and shared responsibility. My deepest concern today is that we are losing these opportunities, as many noble Lords have mentioned. Too many young people are absorbed in social media, simply rei
contributions.name: Baroness Gill

contributions.text: My Lords, our 16 and 17 year-olds are to be given the vote and there are around 1.5 million of them. This is at a time when our politics have never been so febrile and unpredictable. There is therefore a burning question as to whether our young people are equipped with the knowledge they need to use their vote in an informed way, or even want to vote at all. The good news is that citizenship education is already part of the national curriculum at key stages 3 and 4. This says that pupils “should” be taught about democratic government, the key elements of the UK constitution, human rights, financial matters, a free press, et cetera. But it is one thing to write these things into the national curriculum and quite another to deliver them in practice. Many pupils are not being taught these things at all or there is insufficient attention given to their importance, which explains why Professor Becky Francis’s review of the national curriculum found a less than 5% take-up of citizenship at GCSE, as the noble Lord, Lord Norton, has pointed out. There should be more teachers trained in citizenship issues who can teach the subject in an impartial and engaging way in every school. As the nob
contributions.name: Lord Carter of Haslemere

contributions.text: My Lords, the lack of specialist teachers for citizenship, as my noble friend Lord Norton outlined, means that schools have had to be super-flexible in how they teach this subject. In some schools, it is a stand-alone, with a few going on to GCSE; in some, it is taught across the curriculum in history, RE and politics; in some, it is merged with PHSE; in some, it is part of the pastoral curriculum taught first thing in the morning in forms; and in some, it is taught as part of fundamental British values. Such flexibility is not necessarily a bad thing. When the charity Freedom Declared Foundation, of which I am a trustee, together with Regent’s Park College in Oxford—in which I must declare an interest—sought to create secondary school resources on freedom of religion or belief in the UK with RE teachers, the teachers arrived equipped with the exam board curriculums in citizenship and neatly slotted it in. My main question to His Majesty’s Government is this: how much emphasis is there, whether at primary or at secondary, on why we are a democracy? Encouraging young people to vote and volunteer is necessary, but when algorithms are sending mainly boys to the glorification of the st
contributions.name: Baroness Berridge

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Norton of Louth, for securing this debate and for his excellent speech. It is a great pleasure to follow my former boss and noble friend Lord Blunkett, who has been such a great advocate on this topic. I speak as a passionate advocate myself for citizenship education and its role in building the resilient, informed and engaged citizens of the future. So how do we get from good intentions to good implementation? First, we must acknowledge some of the problems with the habit of suggesting simply that adding something to the national curriculum solves a problem. We have a smorgasbord of RHSE, PHSE, financial and digital literacy, enterprise education, and so on. While all these demands are perfectly reasonable, the curriculum cannot simply be an ever-growing list of things that politicians and campaigners think are important. There are, therefore, four things I believe we need to do. The first is to understand what is already being taught rather than simply trying to add more and more obligations. The second is to bring these subjects together. What do we want our young people to know and be able to do when they leave school, and why? Let us crea
contributions.name: Lord Doyle

contributions.text: My Lords, I would like to talk about the financial education aspect of citizenship education, which I know the Government are committed to improving. It is imperative that children learn the necessary financial skills for their future. To quote the money-saving expert Martin Lewis, “our children are sent out into a world of scams, dodgy deals and debt, without the tools to cope”. The useful Library briefing for this debate tells us that parents, carers and students are dissatisfied with “the present level of attention on this topic in the curriculum” and that there is “a strong appetite for more”. I draw the attention of the House to a recent report titled Jobs and Investment , published by the Jobs Foundation—a charity of which I am proud to be president, as declared in the register. This included the recommendation for the teaching of basic investment in schools. Teaching practical skills on rates of return, basic portfolio principles and retirement planning would set children up for life—a life of financial stability. We should also teach the power of compound interest, the importance of delayed gratification to future well-being and—dare I say it?—why capital gains have always
contributions.name: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell

contributions.text: My Lords, my commitment to citizenship education was cemented during my time working for the National Citizen Service—NCS—which brought together young people from different backgrounds to help build confidence, forge lasting relationships, and develop a sense of shared purpose, primarily through volunteering in their local communities. NCS often changed young people’s lives and demonstrated to me that citizenship should be an activity and not a subject. We might bear that in mind when we think about future provision. Like the noble Lord, Lord Norton, I will focus on the potential of citizenship education to strengthen our national resilience. Members of this House are acutely aware of the challenges that our country faces and the resulting sense of uncertainty and threat. In that climate, resilience depends on whether people feel that they belong, trust one another and, significantly, trust the institutions that govern them. I worry that we have too little understanding of what many young people are exposed to online and of the malign influences seeking to undermine our values and institutions. Looking at France over the weekend, I refuse to believe that, among the chaos, there is
contributions.name: Baroness Paul of Shepherd’s Bush

contributions.text: My Lords, I welcome this debate and congratulate my noble friend on his tireless work on citizenship education over the years and on his speech today. I serve on your Lordships’ National Resilience Committee and much of our work concerns how the country can withstand threats to its institutions and security. However, national resilience cannot be secured by the state alone; it also depends on the judgment and conduct of citizens. Last week, Sir Ken McCallum urged us to be “clear-eyed about the more contested world we now live in”. This is absolutely right, but being clear-eyed requires more than a recognition of the external threats; it requires the ability to distinguish between credible information and manipulation, and between disagreement and enmity. Citizenship education must therefore go beyond teaching how Parliament and elections work. Young people should understand why the rule of law matters, how to assess evidence and how to disagree without treating others as enemies. These are essential disciplines of democratic life and national resilience. I welcome the Government’s plans to extend compulsory citizenship education to primary schools in England from 2028 and to streng
contributions.name: Baroness Helic

contributions.text: My Lords, when, in a recent poll, UK adults were asked to identify approximate annual government spending, only 16% selected the correct answer. In another poll, when people were asked about their understanding of how laws were made, 49% said they knew not very much about, knew nothing about or had never heard of the process. These figures raise an important question: how can we expect people to participate meaningfully in our democracy if they do not understand how it works? As citizenship education is expanded, particularly into primary schools, we should focus not simply on what children will be taught but on how they are taught it. The ability to think critically, weigh competing arguments and understand their responsibility to the communities in which they live should run throughout the entire curriculum. Those of us who have spent our lives in public policy know that politics is fundamentally about trade-offs, balancing competing priorities and considering unintended consequences. We should equip children with the skills to navigate these choices thoughtfully. How they apply what they know is just as important as what they know. Citizenship education must be more than a box-t
contributions.name: Baroness Porter of Fulwood

contributions.text: My Lords, to be effective, education must go beyond mere description of a sociopolitical system and include critique. Young people must be shown that democracy is preferable to plutocracy and that it must be protected from the power of corporations and the super-rich who buy the political system and hire legislators. The syllabus must encourage students to design community-based projects and see for themselves the effects of inequalities which deprive millions of nutritious food, good housing, health care, education and pensions. Such projects must consider why elected Governments are content with 1% of the population owning more wealth than 70% of the population combined; why the state forces the poorest 20% to pay a higher proportion of their income in direct and indirect taxes than the richest 20%; and why our Government are content with fiscal rules which send 300,000 people a year to premature death due to lack of timely hospital appointments. Galbraith’s book, The Culture of Contentment , ought to be essential reading, as it explains how the rising affluence of the few has shaped the politics of selfishness and hypocrisy and the hollowing out of economies and democracie
contributions.name: Lord Sikka

contributions.text: My Lords, it was a pleasure to be part of the 2018 committee that looked at citizenship under the chairmanship of Lord Hodgson of Astley Abbotts. Although it has taken nearly 10 years, it is pleasing to see that the Government are finally getting around to responding positively to some of the suggestions we made then. I should also say that I spend a lot of time talking to schoolchildren in our education centre, and I very much welcome the move to extend citizenship education to primary schools, because the level of engagement, interest and desire for further knowledge from very young children is a constant surprise and delight to me. Going back to the committee, one of the biggest disappointments we had was Ofsted’s then lack of interest in citizenship teaching: it really was not interested in seeing that schools were being assessed on the level or quality of their teaching, and teachers were having to make up curricula in their own time and with their own resources. I am really glad that we are going to move away from that and towards proper standardisation. I am also pleased that we are going to stop mixing up citizenship with PSHE and a whole gaggle of other things. I was criti
contributions.name: Baroness Barker

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Norton of Louth, for securing this debate. It was really terrible to see France burning this weekend and watch Limoges Hall fall, with at least two dead so far. It began with rioting schoolchildren. Here in the UK, we have recent polling showing that less than half of young Britons support our democratic system. It is a natural reflex to say, “teach citizenship”, but how and what we teach under this subject is of vital importance, because it has gone so badly wrong elsewhere. There is no time to discuss this tonight, but do look at what has happened in Illinois, Massachusetts and Quebec; it has been devastating. Children should be taught our history, our constitution, and equality before the law. Of course they should be taught how to participate; but the content being written by staff in the Department for Education, taught by teachers who are untrained, as we have heard tonight, and without any supervision or oversight as yet known to us by Ofsted or elsewhere, is simply not going to be adequate. We have heard from the noble Baroness, Lady Paul, that about one in six people arrested for counter-terrorism in the UK are children. The noble Bar
contributions.name: Baroness Cash

contributions.who: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions (Baroness Smith of Malvern) (Lab)
contributions.text: My Lords, as others have, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Norton, for securing this important debate on citizenship education. The noble Lord is a leading expert on Parliament and I know that citizenship is very close to his heart. As many noble Lords have said during this short debate, citizenship matters because it is important that young people understand our democratic institutions, their rights and responsibilities and the part they can play in shaping our country— a point emphasised by the noble Lady Baroness, Lady Porter. Citizenship education gives young people the knowledge and confidence to become active, informed and responsible members of society. Citizenship is, of course, already a national curriculum subject, having been introduced under the previous Labour Government when my noble friend Lord Blunkett was the Secretary of State and I was a lowly foot-soldier Minister in helping him to introduce that subject. The statutory content already covers democracy and government, the law and rights, financial education and participation in society, as well as critical thinking and mutual respect. However, that does not mean that we think the status quo is good enough. The Curric
